title: Praise and blame
hook: favor and disgrace both unsettle us; care for the world as for your own body (Tao Te Ching 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was five colors: too much, and the senses go numb. Your line was less to see.

A cook in a busy kitchen gets two messages from the dining room in the same minute. Table four sends compliments to the chef. Table nine sends a plate back. One feels like sun, the other like a cold draft. An hour later, both are still replaying while the next orders wait, both pulling attention off the stove, both quietly handing the steering wheel to someone in the dining room. Chapter thirteen of the Tao Te Ching puts praise and blame side by side and says something odd: they're the same kind of trouble.
screen: `TWO MESSAGES FROM THE DINING ROOM.` → `COMPLIMENTS, AND A PLATE SENT BACK.` → `THE SAME KIND OF TROUBLE.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. Favor and disgrace both startle a person, the chapter opens. Not just disgrace; favor too. When you get favor, you're startled; when you lose it, you're startled again. Praise isn't a resting place. It's a thing you can now lose. Second, why favor unsettles. The chapter calls favor the lower thing, and readers take this more than one way. Some hear: to be favored is to stand beneath whoever does the favoring, so their approval becomes something you need. Others hear simply that favor is worth less than people think. Either way, praise ties you to someone else's opinion as surely as blame does. Third, the body. Then a startling question: why does a person have great troubles? Because they have a body, a self. If there were no self, what trouble could reach them? Some readers hear this not as a call to give up the body, but as pointing at the part of a person that keeps score of how they're seen, where so much distress gathers. Fourth, the turn outward. Whoever values the whole world the way they value their own body, the chapter ends, can be trusted with the world. The care you'd spend guarding your reputation, spend on everything else instead: from how am I seen, to what needs care.
screen: `FAVOR AND DISGRACE BOTH STARTLE.` · `FAVOR IS THE LOWER THING.` · `TROUBLE GATHERS AROUND THE SELF.` · `CARE FOR THE WORLD AS FOR YOUR BODY.` · then, large: `FAVOR AND DISGRACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a recent compliment and notice where it lands in the body: a warmth, a lift, a small wish to hear it again. Don't push it away or hold on; let it pass like a car on the street outside, and if a criticism shows up instead, treat it the same way. Then let your attention turn to one person or one task that needs care.
Praise and blame. In chapter thirteen, favor and disgrace: two sides of one worry, both of them tied to someone else's opinion. Today's word.
Your line: favor and disgrace. Either one can take the steering wheel, if you let it. Day one thousand seventy-five, done.

howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching use chapter thirteen as a check after praise or criticism: they notice how both pull at them, and turn their attention back to the work or the people in front of them.

Tao Te Ching.meaning: the short old Chinese classic this year reads, chapter by chapter

notes: Chapter 13 paraphrased throughout (Legge 1891 not quoted: his rendering opens 'Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared', which the writer could not confirm word for word).

'Favor is the lower thing' (寵為下) is read differently by translators; two readings are given without ranking. Some editions read the line differently (e.g. 'favor is above, disgrace below'); a scholar should check which reading to present.
'Because we have a self to protect' paraphrases 吾所以有大患者，為吾有身 ('because I have a body'); the move from 'body' to 'a self to protect' is interpretive. Confirm it is fair.
The closing lines (one who values the world as his own body can be entrusted with it) are paraphrased; confirm.
